title: A great multitude (Apocalypse 7:9–17)
hook: from all nations, tribes, peoples and tongues; read on All Saints
tomorrow: a woman clothed with the sun

segments.voice: Yesterday, arnion: the Lamb standing with its wounds still showing. Your line was worthy is the lamb.

On the first of November, the Church celebrates All Saints. Not one saint: all of them. The famous ones with statues, and the ones nobody ever canonized: the grandmother who prayed the rosary on the bus, the farmer who never missed Sunday, the nurse who held hands on night shifts. Names no calendar has room for. The first reading at Mass that day comes from Apocalypse seven. It begins with a number, and then John looks up and sees something no number can hold.
screen: `THE FIRST OF NOVEMBER.` → `SAINTS NO CALENDAR CAN HOLD.` → `A NUMBER, THEN A CROWD.`

segments.voice: First John hears a number: a hundred and forty-four thousand, sealed, twelve thousand from each tribe of Israel. Twelve times twelve, times a thousand: Catholic interpreters read it as a symbol of the whole people of God, complete. Then, just as he heard of a lion and saw a lamb, he hears a number and sees a crowd. In the Douay-Rheims: "After this I saw a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and tribes, and peoples, and tongues, standing before the throne, and in sight of the Lamb, clothed with white robes, and palms in their hands." Every accent and alphabet on earth, standing together. Palms in their hands, a sign of victory, like the crowd that waved branches when Jesus rode into Jerusalem. They cry out that salvation belongs to God and to the Lamb. Then an elder asks John: who are these in white, and where did they come from? John, overwhelmed, says simply, "My lord, thou knowest." The elder tells him: "These are they who are come out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and have made them white in the blood of the Lamb." Robes washed in blood come out white. These aren't people who avoided suffering; they came through it. And the chapter ends with a promise for them: no more hunger, no more thirst, no burning sun. The Lamb will be their shepherd and lead them to springs of living water. On All Saints, Catholics remember that this crowd includes people they knew.
screen: `A NUMBER: 144,000.` · `A CROWD NO MAN COULD NUMBER.` · `MY LORD, THOU KNOWEST.` · `WASHED WHITE IN THE BLOOD OF THE LAMB.` · then, large: `ALL NATIONS, AND TRIBES, AND PEOPLES, AND TONGUES.`

segments.voice: Imagine a huge open space before a throne, filling with people from every continent: old women in headscarves, teenagers, farmers, a child holding a palm branch, a man in a wheelchair, languages you don't know. Let it fill until you can't see the edges, then look for someone you knew who has died, a grandparent, a friend, a teacher, in white, holding a palm. If you pray, you can ask them to pray for you; if not, just let yourself see them there.
A great multitude. Apocalypse seven: a crowd no one could count, from every nation and tongue, in white before the Lamb. Today's word.
Your line: every tongue. Every nation, every language, one cry of praise. Day six hundred twenty-six.

screen: `DAY 626 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A WOMAN CLOTHED WITH THE SUN.`

howItsDone: On the Solemnity of All Saints, November 1, Catholics hear Apocalypse 7 at Mass and honor all the saints, known and unknown; the next day, All Souls, they pray for all the faithful departed.

what it means: John hears a number, then sees a crowd no one can count, from every nation and tongue: the saints, known and unknown.
what a scholar hears: hearing and then seeing, like the lion and the Lamb in chapter 5; 144,000 is twelve times twelve times a thousand, the people of God made complete.
